extracted.intended_audience: law professors, patent lawyers, judges, and advanced law students studying patent claim construction and legal theory
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for analyzing and deciding patent claim meaning and scope, distinguishing linguistic interpretation from normative construction, and for choosing institutional procedures and evidentiary sources in claim construction disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation–construction distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Separate the question of what the claim language linguistically means (interpretation) from the question of what legal effect or scope the claim should have (construction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat interpretation as addressing factual linguistic meaning (what people in the art actually understand the language to communicate) and construction as the normative decision about whether the linguistic meaning should govern patent scope; use this distinction as a conceptual tool to expose the real sources of dispute and to frame policy debates cleanly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish linguistic uncertainty from legal/policy uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not assume that uncertainty over patent rights primarily stems from ambiguity in claim language; uncertainty often arises from judges' normative disagreements over whether to follow linguistic meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that most prominent claim-construction disputes are methodological (textualism vs anti-textualism) rather than genuine disputes about linguistic content; thus efforts to refine linguistic tools will often not resolve the core problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of linguistic tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Better or more sophisticated linguistic analysis cannot by itself resolve methodological disagreements about claim scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because many disputes are about whether the linguistic meaning should govern (a policy choice), sharper linguistic techniques will be of limited help; scholars and judges should avoid presenting policy choices as technical linguistic inevitabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: When courts should look beyond the text (vagueness / construction zone)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts must look beyond the claim text only in the limited circumstance where the claim is genuinely vague and the dispute falls within the 'construction zone.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If true vagueness exists, policy considerations necessarily come into play and courts should acknowledge and resolve them; avoid treating that narrow category as proof that courts should routinely ignore claim text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper sources for discerning claim meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts may consult internal and external evidence—specification, prosecution history, dictionaries, and expert testimony—to discern what claim language means to those skilled in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases differ on the preferred order and weight of these sources (see Phillips, Telegenix, Multiform); for technical terms the specification is often the best source, while other authorities (dictionaries, experts) may be appropriate depending on context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not conflate linguistic meaning with the patentee’s invention
rubrics_metrics.description: A difference between the linguistic meaning of claim text and the patentee's conception of the invention is not itself a linguistic ambiguity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid the rhetorical move of treating every divergence between written claims and the 'real' invention as textual ambiguity; many so-called 'ambiguities' reflect a normative choice about whether to enforce patentee-drafted text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-textualist proposals are policy arguments (not linguistic necessities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments for looking to the 'real' invention (or abolishing claims) are fundamentally normative: they aim to produce narrower, less patentee-favorable scopes to correct biased drafting incentives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-textualist scholars should state these normative goals openly rather than masking them as inevitable consequences of linguistic indeterminacy; doing so clarifies the true debate and invites explicit policy adjudication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for patentee drafting incentives and bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentees have an incentive to draft claims broadly and self-servingly, which motivates proposals to discount claim text in favor of a neutral judge's conception of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider these incentive effects when evaluating methodological proposals, but treat them as policy tradeoffs that must be justified normatively rather than as proof of textual indeterminacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional allocation: legal question vs factual question
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim interpretation involves factual elements (what PHOSITA understand) but has been doctrinally classified (Markman) as a 'purely legal' question for appellate resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the mixed nature: while interpretation implicates factual inquiry, there are normative and doctrinal reasons to treat claim-construction methodology as primarily a legal (appellate) question to promote doctrinal consistency and settle methodology at the appellate level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of review and deference issues
rubrics_metrics.description: There is debate whether claim construction should be reviewed de novo on appeal or receive deference to district-court factual findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh competing arguments: de novo review supports uniform methodology from appellate courts; some scholars advocate deference for factual predicates (expert evidence) and a hybrid approach may be appropriate depending on documentary vs factual sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims are the measure of the patent grant (public notice function)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent claims, not specifications, ordinarily define the bounds of the patentee's rights and serve the public-notice function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect the default rule that claim language frames and resolves issues of interpretation; any departure (e.g., equity-based narrowing) requires explicit normative justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of equivalents is a narrow exception to the claim-as-written rule
rubrics_metrics.description: A court may find infringement under the doctrine of equivalents when an accused product differs only insubstantially from the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the doctrine as a limited judicial tool rather than a license to routinely override claim text; its availability does not justify broad anti-textualist approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolve vagueness candidly to avoid empty interpretations
rubrics_metrics.description: When courts face genuine vagueness, they should acknowledge that claim text cannot resolve the issue and that policy considerations will decide outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to do so produces empty 'interpretations' that leave outcomes to juries or hidden reasoning; explicit recognition of the policy choice leads to clearer, more accountable decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Argue claim-construction methodology overtly on policy grounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Both textualists and anti-textualists should make explicit normative arguments for their preferred methodologies rather than cloaking them as purely linguistic conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open normative debate fosters clearer conceptual analysis and better scholarly engagement; it prevents the rhetorical concealment of policy choices behind claims of linguistic inevitability.
